name: Guatemala
summary: Heartland of the ancient Maya; independent in 1821; a US-backed coup (1954) led to a civil war (1960–96) in which about 200,000 died, mostly Maya.

location.value: A country in northern Central America.

terrain.value: Volcanic highlands (37 volcanoes, four of them active) and hot tropical lowlands.

climate.value: Hot, humid tropical lowlands and colder, drier highland peaks.

resources.value: Coffee, bananas, sugar, cardamom and nickel.

disasters.value: A major earthquake on 4 February 1976 killed more than 25,000 people; active volcanoes include Fuego.

urbanisation.value: Guatemala City, the capital, has the most populous metropolitan area in Central America.

disease.value: Around a quarter of the population (4.6 million) face food insecurity.

migration.value: Many Guatemalans live in the United States; the money they send home is the country's largest single source of foreign income.

economicBase.value: Remittances from Guatemalans in the United States are the largest single source of foreign income (19% of GDP in 2024).

tradeRoutes.value: Ports on both the Atlantic and Pacific coasts carry exports, mostly to the United States.

wealth.value: Poor and unequal: 56% lived in poverty and 16.2% in extreme poverty in 2024.

moneyAndTax.value: The quetzal, named for the national bird.

keyRulers.value: Rafael Carrera. Jacobo Árbenz. Efraín Ríos Montt.

institutions.value: The UN-backed International Commission against Impunity in Guatemala (CICIG) helped prosecutors expose corruption.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

majorWars.value: The Guatemalan Civil War (1960–1996), ended by a UN-negotiated peace accord.

territoryChange.value: Has long claimed all or part of Belize; it recognised Belize's independence only in 1991, and the dispute is not resolved.

alliancesRivals.value: A member of the Central American Integration System and the United Nations.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: Low literacy rates, partly because rural teachers lack training.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Roads and the Pan-American Highway; the railways have largely closed.

religion.value: Christian: between 2001 and 2012 Catholics fell from 55% to 47.9% and Protestants grew from 30% to 38.2%.

languageWriting.value: Spanish is the sole official language; 21 Mayan languages are also spoken.

artsArchitecture.value: Maya art and architecture, and the colonial city of Antigua Guatemala.

socialStructure.value: 56% Ladino and 43.6% Indigenous, most of them Maya (2018 census).

dailyLife.value: Many families eat tortillas and beans, and Maya communities keep weaving and market traditions.

ideasReligions.value: A revival of Mayan languages and bilingual education.

colonisation.value: Part of the Captaincy General of Guatemala, within the Spanish Viceroyalty of New Spain, until 1821.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Guatemala continues as an independent republic.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
